Escaping Afghanistan

By: Anina Peens | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Hundreds of South Africans are stuck in Afghanistan while the Taliban is taking control of the country and South Africa has no plans to send expatriation flights.

Unique Selling Point:
While thousands of people stormed the airport in Kabul to escape a country that has been taken over by an extremist terrorist group, many South Africans were stuck in hotels, waiting on help to flee war-torn Afghanistan.

Summary:
Nicky Venter worked in a hotel in Kabul, Afghanistan and was as surprised by the sudden Taliban take-over as were many world powers. He had no plans to exit the country but when president Ashraf Ghani and his government suddenly fled, he was stuck, along with many other South African citizens. The rush to flee the country saw thousands desperately flock to the airport in Kabul, grabbing onto planes, eager to get out. The Taliban warned upon taking over, that those who choose to remain in the country will be forced to live under Sharia law. Venter and other South Africans waited in their hotels to be expatriated back home while bullets rained over the city.

Further information:
On the eve of the 20th anniversary of the attack on the World Trade center, the Taliban is celebrating victory.
The rise of fundamentalism finally succeeded in Afghanistan, and this will have significant consequences for other fundamentalists operating across the world including Mozambique, our direct neighbor.
If looking at the problems of others, yours may not seem so bad.
Those who are unable to flee will be forced to live under Sharia law, enforced by the Taliban. Women will have no rights and all the progress made with women emancipation under extremist Islam laws over the last twenty years, is now lost.
So what exactly is Sharia law and why are people so afraid?
Also, how do local South African Muslims feel about the turn of events?

Script:


DECADE OF DROUGHT FINAL 8 SEPTEMBER

VO
Namaqualand’s flower spectacle belies a hard truth. While light winter rain was enough to set the iconic flowers ablaze, once the colour carpet wilts, the earth is too barren to yield food. Extreme weather events are a sign of climate change. Abroad, Germany and China had unprecedented floods, England heatwaves and America hurricanes. While these disasters come fast and cause sudden destruction, the drought is a slow process of eradication.
The Western, Eastern and Northern Cape, have been fighting for survival for nearly a decade. During the last two years, the Western parts of the Northern Cape received only about 25 millimetres of rain. Compared to Johannesburg, where residents are used to an average 800 millimetres of rain, annually.

LINK
“Sitting here in suburban Johannesburg, it is hard to just get an idea of what farmers have gone through. Jaco Visagie farms near Calvinia and has managed to keep going, but it has been a heartbreaking struggle”

UPSOUND
PHONE RINGING IN JACO’S KITCHEN
CUT TO DEREK AFTER JACO ANSWERS
DEREK: Hi goeimore Jaco, hoe gaan dit daar op die plaas?
SUPER@ JACO VISAGIE: FARMER, CALVINIA
JACO: “Very good Derek, we finally got some rain and we sure hope it is gonna hold out for a while”
DEREK: That’s great man… but Jaco I want to know a bit about your past when it comes to farming. Does it go back generations? Tell us the story”
Jaco: “So basically, I grew up here and this family farm has been in our family for the last 160 years.”
DEREK: “Now, farmers usually prepare for drought, don’t they? But this was something out of the ordinary?”
JACO: “Derek this is something that is terrible, we never experienced anything like this. My grandfather had a drought in the early 20’s and there was a drought in the 60’s as well. But this time was difficult, the rain just kept away, and it was really difficult to keep everything going. “

VO
This map shows the devastation of sheep farms. The white spots indicate normal vegetation, the dark red, the most extreme form of abnormality.

SUPER@CALLIE VAN ZYL: FARMER: LOERIESFONTEIN
“Hierdie swart knoppe wat hier in die grond sit, dit is graspolle wat gevrek het as gevolg van die droogte. So oral sit sulke droeë gevrekte kolle. So as jy nou hierdie draadjie teen die pad kyk, hy is so drie voet hoog, ‘n meter. As dit nou reg reën dan staan hierdie gras so hoog soos die draad, ‘n meter hoog.”
SUBTITLE
“These black patches are the remnants of grass that died. You can see the patches everywhere. If you look at the fence, it is one meter high. If we get good rain, the grass will be the same height of the fence. But the animals ate everything there was and the rest just died”

VO
Callie Van Zyl farms near Loeriesfontein in the Hantam district. He says, about 20 farmers in his area have given up farming over the last few years.

SUPER@ CALLIE VAN ZYL: FARMER, LOERIESFONTEIN
“Ons sit in ‘n hoop dat dit sal volgende jaar beter wees en volgende jaar wees. En ek dink daai volgende jaar het nou ‘n bietjie te laat gekom.
SUBTITLE
“We keep on hoping that next year will be better or maybe the year after. I think that next year is too late for some farmers”

VO
Van Zyl says the land can only carry sheep and the majority of farmers had to cut down their herds to keep only the core breeding stock. While some farmers try everything to keep their land, one of the biggest concerns is that the drought is scaring potential new farmers away.

SUPER@ CALLIE VAN ZYL: FARMER: LOERIESFONTEIN
“So, hier het jong mense gebly waaroor ons baie bly was dat hulle hier kom intrek het, want ons gemeenskap is geneig om baie ouer te raak omdat daar nie mense terug kom nie. Maar nou ja, na ‘n paar jaar staan die huisie ook nou leeg, hier woon nie meer iemand nie en dit was ook mense wat baie aspirasies gehad het”
SUBTITLE
This land has a way of kicking you off especially if a drought lasts this long. So, young people moved into this house, and we were very happy about that because our community is aging as young people don’t come home to farm. Now, this house is also abandoned and the people who lived here had great aspirations”

LINK
“If more farmers leave the sector, the price of red meat goes up and putting chops on the braai may become a luxury.”

VO
But it does not end there. According to AGRI SA, the affected areas of the Northern Cape region create about 10 thousand permanent jobs and a further 20 thousand down the value chain. This is specifically for unskilled or low skilled workers. All the small towns in the province are dependent on two major forms of income, agriculture, and grants and effects of the drought is visible across the Northern Cape.

VO
Like many depend on SASSA, hundreds of farmers now live off donations. Not only for fodder but food for their families. Hennie Pieterse, travels to the Northern Cape from Rustenburg biweekly to distribute donations from across the country.

SUPER@ HENNIE PIETERSE: VOER VIR ‘N BOER
1’18”
“Currently we’re running two, three trucks a week up to Pofadder or Loeriesfontein, depends on where the most feed is needed.”
00’44”
“We have a couple of farmers that we try to sustain. We try to sustain them for the next year or two years, until the rain comes or until there is relief”.

VO
Koolie Farmer also farms sheep in the Hantam. He says while donations help farmers to keep their land, the psychological impact of the drought is enduring.

SUPER@KOLIE FARMER: FARMER: LOERIESFONTEIN
“Hy breek jou emosioneel af, hy breek jou sielkindig af. Ek meen, nege jaar is ‘n lang tyd en hy is nog nie oor nie. En soos hierdie blommetjies wat ons hier sien, dit is nie die oplossing nie want net oor twee maande is hier nie een blommetjie nie dan is ons weer terug en ons het nie ‘n oplossing nie”
SUBTITLES
“It breaks you down on an emotional and psycological level. I mean, nine years is a long time, and it is not over yet. En now, you see the flowers here but that is not the solution because in two months’ time they are gone, and we still don’t have a solution.”

LINK
The national disaster management centre classified the drought as a national disaster on the 20th of July this year. But there is a big difference between a classification and declaration and so far, there has been no declaration.

VO
Dr Mmpakha Tau is the man at the steer of the center. He says that when a disaster is classified, provincial government structures must treat the disaster as priority.

SUPER@ DR MMAPHAKA TAU: NAT. DISASTER MANAGEMENT CENTRE: HEAD
“Tapping into the base line of the sector department is where a department of agriculture will use their funds to make sure that they support farmers in adaptation practices”

VO
But the Northern Cape government declined to comment on relief efforts in the absence of an official declaration. Agri SA says, provincial budgets are not big enough for proper assistance and national treasury does not budget sufficiently for disaster.

VO
SUPER@ANDREA CAMPHER: DISASTER RELIEF: AGRI SA
“National government mobilizes funding to provincial departments and then to local governments. But at the end of the day, we don’t see that that money reaches the farmer.”

VO
Koolie Farmer says farmers are frustrated with the lack of interest on the side of government.

SUPER@KOLIE FARMER: FARMER: LOERIESFONTEIN
“Dit is mos vanselfsprekend. As belastingbetaler verwag jy mos nou dat die een vir wie jy jou belastinggelde gee en wat die beloftes maak, hulle moet nou mos na vore kom in die moeilike tyd maar jinne. Maar as jy nou luister, weet ek nie of die regte manne in die regte stoele is nie. Of hulle harte in hierdie area is nie”
SUBTITLE
“It is obvious. As a taxpayer, you expect that the one you are paying your taxes to and those who make promises must be there for you during difficult times, but alas. If I look at the situation, I don’t know if the right people are in the right chairs. Their hearts are not in it”

VO
Dr Tau says government can’t be the answer for survival.

SUPER@ DR MMAPHAKA TAU: NAT. DISASTER MANAGEMENT CENTRE: HEAD
“Let our people adopt a new paradigm of managing risk in their area. Because it is not sustainable or affordable that you can use response as a mainstay for sustaining farming. Adaptation, adaptation is the key to succeed.”

VO
Nomadic in nature, Hantam farmers move their sheep between winter and summer rainfall areas. But since 2011, there has not been sufficient rain in either region and adaptation is found in alternative possibilities. Visagie started to work as farm manager in America to keep his own farm back home. But this was a massive sacrifice.

SUPER@ JACO VISAGIE: FARMER, CALVINA
“I enjoyed working over there but it is far away, and you lose so much time spending with your family”

VO
Between 2013 and 2019 he traveled to America regularly and stayed away for periods of six to eight months. In the meantime, he was experimenting with onion crops back home and his wife Rozenda had to manage the farm.

SUPER@ ROZENDA VISAGIE: JACO’S WIFE
“Me and my son had to stay, two years old and ja it was very hard for me to explain to him where his dad is going. And I had to stay behind because we had onions in the ground and they needed to be looked after and we had sheep”

VO
Rozenda is originally from Cape Town and had to adapt fast into her role as onion farmer.

SUPER@ ROZENDA VISAGIE: JACO’S WIFE
“The hardest part for me was working with the farmers people because they thought that I am a woman and I don’t know much…it is very easy to see Jaco do stuff and think ahh it is not that bad, I can do it. But when you do it yourself, it is not that easy”

VO
According to Agri SA’s research, the drought is still far from over .

SUPER@ANDREA CAMPHER: DISASTER RELIEF: AGRI SA
“There will be more agricultural drought in the coming year and we know that these provinces, the Western Cape, Eastern Cape and Northern Cape are now facing the sixth to ninth year of the drought and therefore the prospects are not that good.”

VO
The Visagies say, they will do whatever it takes to keep their land.

SUPER@ ROZENDA VISAGIE: JACO’S WIFE
“We have spoken about Jaco leaving for America again and we hope and pray that it doesn’t have to, we have the onions in the ground for now and that can carry us so we hope he doesn’t have to go again.”

DEREK: “Jaco, do you sometimes sit on the stoep and feel that you have just been forgotten by South Africa?”
SUPER@ JACO VISAGIE: FARMER: CALVINIA
“I do. I feel like, we are trying our best to provide for the country, but then you are battling with this drought and there is nothing anybody could do for you. You are on your own and you’re battling your own fights, and it is difficult.




21”
The flower season of the Namaqualand attracts tourists every year to bask in the beauty. But when they leave and the flowers wilt, the barren earth provides no food for those staying behind. How has the extended drought impacted farmers who’ve had to adapt or pack up and leave?

21”
It’s the ninth year of a devastating drought in the Northern Cape, seventh in the Eastern and Western Cape. While donations help some farmers survive – others have made great sacrifices to hold onto their land, while government says long-term aid is unsustainable. How have some farmers embraces new ways of living to fend off total destruction?


11”
As drought in parts of the Northern, Eastern and Western Cape stretches toward the decade mark – with millions of hectares of land devastated - what is the impact on farmers and their community?

But there is a big difference between a classification and declaration and so far, there has been no declaration. VO Dr Mmpakha Tau is the man at the steer of the center. He says that when a disaster is classified, provincial government structures must treat the disaster as priority. SUPER@ DR MMAPHAKA TAU: NAT. DISASTER MANAGEMENT CENTRE: HEAD “Tapping into the base line of the sector department is where a department of agriculture will use their funds to make sure that they support farmers in adaptation practices” VO But the Northern Cape government declined to comment on relief efforts in the absence of an official declaration. Agri SA says, provincial budgets are not big enough for proper assistance and national treasury does not budget sufficiently for disaster. VO SUPER@ANDREA CAMPHER: DISASTER RELIEF: AGRI SA “National government mobilizes funding to provincial departments and then to local governments. But at the end of the day, we don’t see that that money reaches the farmer.” VO Koolie Farmer says farmers are frustrated with the lack of interest on the side of government. SUPER@KOLIE FARMER: FARMER: LOERIESFONTEIN “Dit is mos vanselfsprekend. As belastingbetaler verwag jy mos nou dat die een vir wie jy jou belastinggelde gee en wat die beloftes maak, hulle moet nou mos na vore kom in die moeilike tyd maar jinne. Maar as jy nou luister, weet ek nie of die regte manne in die regte stoele is nie. Of hulle harte in hierdie area is nie” SUBTITLE “It is obvious. As a taxpayer, you expect that the one you are paying your taxes to and those who make promises must be there for you during difficult times, but alas. If I look at the situation, I don’t know if the right people are in the right chairs. Their hearts are not in it” VO Dr Tau says government can’t be the answer for survival. SUPER@ DR MMAPHAKA TAU: NAT. DISASTER MANAGEMENT CENTRE: HEAD “Let our people adopt a new paradigm of managing risk in their area. Because it is not sustainable or affordable that you can use response as a mainstay for sustaining farming. Adaptation, adaptation is the key to succeed.” VO Nomadic in nature, Hantam farmers move their sheep between winter and summer rainfall areas. But since 2011, there has not been sufficient rain in either region and adaptation is found in alternative possibilities. Visagie started to work as farm manager in America to keep his own farm back home. But this was a massive sacrifice. SUPER@ JACO VISAGIE: FARMER, CALVINA “I enjoyed working over there but it is far away, and you lose so much time spending with your family” VO Between 2013 and 2019 he traveled to America regularly and stayed away for periods of six to eight months. In the meantime, he was experimenting with onion crops back home and his wife Rozenda had to manage the farm. SUPER@ ROZENDA VISAGIE: JACO’S WIFE “Me and my son had to stay, two years old and ja it was very hard for me to explain to him where his dad is going. And I had to stay behind because we had onions in the ground and they needed to be looked after and we had sheep” VO Rozenda is originally from Cape Town and had to adapt fast into her role as onion farmer. SUPER@ ROZENDA VISAGIE: JACO’S WIFE “The hardest part for me was working with the farmers people because they thought that I am a woman and I don’t know much…it is very easy to see Jaco do stuff and think ahh it is not that bad, I can do it. But when you do it yourself, it is not that easy” VO According to Agri SA’s research, the drought is still far from over . SUPER@ANDREA CAMPHER: DISASTER RELIEF: AGRI SA “There will be more agricultural drought in the coming year and we know that these provinces, the Western Cape, Eastern Cape and Northern Cape are now facing the sixth to ninth year of the drought and therefore the prospects are not that good.” VO The Visagies say, they will do whatever it takes to keep their land. SUPER@ ROZENDA VISAGIE: JACO’S WIFE “We have spoken about Jaco leaving for America again and we hope and pray that it doesn’t have to, we have the onions in the ground for now and that can carry us so we hope he doesn’t have to go again.” DEREK: “Jaco, do you sometimes sit on the stoep and feel that you have just been forgotten by South Africa?” SUPER@ JACO VISAGIE: FARMER: CALVINIA “I do. I feel like, we are trying our best to provide for the country, but then you are battling with this drought and there is nothing anybody could do for you. You are on your own and you’re battling your own fights, and it is difficult. 21” The flower season of the Namaqualand attracts tourists every year to bask in the beauty. But when they leave and the flowers wilt, the barren earth provides no food for those staying behind. How has the extended drought impacted farmers who’ve had to adapt or pack up and leave? 21” It’s the ninth year of a devastating drought in the Northern Cape, seventh in the Eastern and Western Cape. While donations help some farmers survive – others have made great sacrifices to hold onto their land, while government says long-term aid is unsustainable. How have some farmers embraces new ways of living to fend off total destruction? 11” As drought in parts of the Northern, Eastern and Western Cape stretches toward the decade mark – with millions of hectares of land devastated - what is the impact on farmers and their community?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Hundreds of South Africans are stuck in Afghanistan while the Taliban is taking control of the country and South Africa has no plans to send expatriation flights.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: While thousands of people stormed the airport in Kabul to escape a country that has been taken over by an extremist terrorist group, many South Africans were stuck in hotels, waiting on help to flee war-torn Afghanistan.
metadata.Summary: Nicky Venter worked in a hotel in Kabul, Afghanistan and was as surprised by the sudden Taliban take-over as were many world powers. He had no plans to exit the country but when president Ashraf Ghani and his government suddenly fled, he was stuck, along with many other South African citizens. The rush to flee the country saw thousands desperately flock to the airport in Kabul, grabbing onto planes, eager to get out. The Taliban warned upon taking over, that those who choose to remain in the country will be forced to live under Sharia law. Venter and other South Africans waited in their hotels to be expatriated back home while bullets rained over the city.
metadata.Further information: On the eve of the 20th anniversary of the attack on the World Trade center, the Taliban is celebrating victory. The rise of fundamentalism finally succeeded in Afghanistan, and this will have significant consequences for other fundamentalists operating across the world including Mozambique, our direct neighbor. If looking at the problems of others, yours may not seem so bad. Those who are unable to flee will be forced to live under Sharia law, enforced by the Taliban. Women will have no rights and all the progress made with women emancipation under extremist Islam laws over the last twenty years, is now lost. So what exactly is Sharia law and why are people so afraid? Also, how do local South African Muslims feel about the turn of events?
